questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The nuclear radius of an Aluminum-27 nucleus is measured to be approximately 3.6 fm. Based on the empirical rule for nuclear radii, what is the approximate nuclear radius of a Tellurium-125 nucleus?
questions.explanation: The empirical formula for nuclear radius is R = R₀ A^(1/3), where A is the mass number. Form a ratio for the two nuclei: R_Te / R_Al = (A_Te / A_Al)^(1/3). Substitute the mass numbers: R_Te / 3.6 = (125 / 27)^(1/3). Evaluating the cube roots gives R_Te / 3.6 = 5 / 3. Solve for R_Te: R_Te = 3.6 × (5/3) = 6.0 fm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Atomic masses and composition of nucleus
questions.question: Which of the following pairs of nuclides represents a pair of strictly defined isotones?
questions.explanation: Isotones are strictly defined as atomic nuclei that have the exact same number of neutrons (N), but different numbers of protons (Z). Number of neutrons N = A - Z. For ¹⁴₆C: N = 14 - 6 = 8 neutrons. For ¹⁶₈O: N = 16 - 8 = 8 neutrons. Since both possess exactly 8 neutrons, they are isotones.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The strong nuclear force between two isolated nucleons (proton-proton, neutron-neutron, or proton-neutron) exhibits which of the following characteristic properties?
options: It is repulsive at all separation distances.
It becomes strongly repulsive at separation distances smaller than roughly 0.7 fm.
It strictly obeys an inverse-square law for macroscopic distances.
It is significantly stronger between two protons than between two neutrons due to added charge.
questions.explanation: The strong nuclear force is intensely attractive at average nucleon separation distances (around 1 fm). However, if nucleons are pushed too close together (less than ~0.7 fm), the nuclear force becomes powerfully repulsive, forming a repulsive core that prevents the nucleus from collapsing. It is strictly charge-independent and does not obey the inverse-square law.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: When a heavy radioactive nucleus undergoes a standard alpha (α) decay, what happens to its neutron-to-proton ratio (N/Z)?
options: It fluctuates unpredictably depending on the specific isotope.
questions.explanation: In an alpha decay, the daughter nucleus loses 2 neutrons and 2 protons. For heavy nuclei, N > Z. Subtracting the same constant (2) from both the numerator (N) and denominator (Z) of a fraction strictly greater than 1 causes the total value of the fraction to algebraically increase.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Which of the following specific nuclei possesses the absolute highest binding energy per nucleon, making it the most tightly bound nucleus in the universe?
questions.explanation: The curve of Binding Energy per nucleon (BE/A) versus Mass Number (A) peaks heavily in the mass region around A ≈ 56. Iron-56 (⁵⁶Fe) has an experimentally measured binding energy per nucleon of approximately 8.8 MeV/nucleon, making it the most thermodynamically stable nucleus.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: One atomic mass unit (1 u) is defined as exactly 1/12th of the rest mass of an unbound neutral atom of Carbon-12. What is the approximate macroscopic energy equivalent of exactly 1 gram (1 g) of pure rest mass?
questions.explanation: Using Einstein's mass-energy equivalence principle, E = mc². Mass m = 1 gram = 10⁻³ kg. Speed of light c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. E = (10⁻³ kg) × (3 × 10⁸ m/s)² = 10⁻³ × 9 × 10¹⁶ = 9 × 10¹³ Joules.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: How many total alpha (α) particles and beta-minus (β⁻) particles are sequentially emitted during the complete transformation of one ²³⁸₉₂U nucleus into one ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb nucleus?
questions.explanation: Total change in mass number ΔA = 238 - 206 = 32. Since only alpha particles alter the mass number (by 4), the number of alpha particles is N_α = 32 / 4 = 8. Emission of 8 alpha particles drops the atomic number (Z) by 16. Expected Z after pure alpha decay = 92 - 16 = 76. To increase Z from 76 back up to the target 82, the nucleus must emit beta-minus particles. Number of beta particles N_β = 82 - 76 = 6.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The half-life of ²³⁸U is approximately 4.5 × 10⁹ years. A geologist analyzes an ancient rock sample and finds that the atomic ratio of ²³⁸U to ²⁰⁶Pb trapped inside it is exactly 1 : 3. Assuming the rock contained absolutely no Lead-206 when it first formed, what is the approximate age of the rock?
questions.explanation: The atomic ratio of U-238 to Pb-206 is 1 : 3. This implies that for every 1 Uranium nucleus remaining, 3 have decayed into Lead. Total original Uranium = 1 + 3 = 4 parts. The fraction of Uranium remaining today is N/N₀ = 1/4. Since 1/4 = (1/2)², exactly 2 half-lives have elapsed. Age of the rock t = 2 × T_1/2 = 2 × (4.5 × 10⁹) = 9.0 × 10⁹ years.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The first step in this chain is the alpha decay of ²³⁸U into Thorium-234 (²³⁴Th). Given the exact atomic masses: ²³⁸U = 238.05079 u, ²³⁴Th = 234.04363 u, and ⁴He = 4.00260 u. What is the approximate energy released (Q-value) in this single specific decay step? (1 u ≈ 931.5 MeV)
questions.explanation: The Q-value for the decay is driven entirely by the mass defect: Q = (M_reactants - M_products) c². Mass of reactants: M_U = 238.05079 u. Mass of products: M_Th + M_He = 234.04363 + 4.00260 = 238.04623 u. Mass defect Δm = 238.05079 - 238.04623 = 0.00456 u. Convert to energy: Q = 0.00456 u × 931.5 MeV/u ≈ 4.247 MeV. Closest approximation is 4.25 MeV.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A nuclear physicist models a typical atomic nucleus as a sphere of uniform density. What is the approximate order of magnitude of the bulk mass density of standard nuclear matter?
questions.explanation: Nuclear volume V = (4/3)πR₀³A. The constant R₀ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Nuclear mass M ≈ A × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Density ρ = M/V. The mass number A cancels out perfectly. ρ ≈ (1.66 × 10⁻²⁷) / ((4/3)π(1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵)³) ≈ 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³. The standard order of magnitude is universally 10¹⁷ kg/m³.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A commercial nuclear fission reactor generates thermal power at a steady rate of 1000 MW. If each individual fission of a Uranium-235 nucleus releases 200 MeV of usable thermal energy, approximately how many fission events must occur inside the reactor core every single second? (1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J)
questions.explanation: Total Thermal Power Output P_th = 1000 MW = 10⁹ J/s. Usable energy released per individual fission E_f = 200 MeV = 200 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J. Fission rate (events per second) = (Total Power) / (Energy per fission) = 10⁹ / (3.2 × 10⁻¹¹) = 3.125 × 10¹⁹ s⁻¹.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A freshly prepared solution contains a mixture of two purely radioactive isotopes, A and B. Isotope A has a half-life of 1 hour, and Isotope B has a half-life of 2 hours. At t = 0, the measured activities of A and B in the solution are exactly equal. What will be the mathematical ratio of the activity of Isotope A to the activity of Isotope B after exactly 4 hours have elapsed?
questions.explanation: Activity follows the radioactive decay law: A(t) = A₀ (1/2)ⁿ, where n is the number of half-lives. Initially at t=0, A_0A = A_0B = A₀. For Isotope A (T_1/2 = 1 hr): After 4 hours, n_A = 4 half-lives. Activity A_A = A₀ (1/2)⁴ = A₀ / 16. For Isotope B (T_1/2 = 2 hr): After 4 hours, n_B = 2 half-lives. Activity A_B = A₀ (1/2)² = A₀ / 4. The ratio of activities after 4 hours is A_A / A_B = (A₀ / 16) / (A₀ / 4) = 4 / 16 = 1 / 4.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The mean life (τ) of a specific radioactive sample characterizes its exponential decay. What exact percentage of the original radioactive nuclei will strictly *decay* (disappear) during a time interval equal to one mean life?
questions.explanation: The radioactive decay law defines the number of undecayed nuclei as N(t) = N₀ e^(-λt). The mean life is precisely defined as τ = 1/λ. Substitute t = τ = 1/λ: The remaining nuclei N(τ) = N₀ e^(-λ(1/λ)) = N₀ e⁻¹. Since e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368, roughly 36.8% of the original nuclei remain undecayed. The percentage that will strictly *decay* is 100% - 36.8% = 63.2%.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A heavy nucleus Y (mass number A = 200) naturally fissions into two identical lighter nuclei X (mass number A = 100). The average binding energy per nucleon of nucleus Y is 8.0 MeV, and the average binding energy per nucleon of nucleus X is 8.5 MeV. What is the total energy released during this specific fission event?
questions.explanation: Total binding energy of parent Y is BE_Y = A_Y × (BE/A)_Y = 200 × 8.0 MeV = 1600 MeV. Total binding energy of two identical daughters X is BE_X = 2 × [A_X × (BE/A)_X] = 2 ×[100 × 8.5 MeV] = 1700 MeV. Energy released (Q-value) is the absolute difference in final vs initial total binding energies: Q = BE_final - BE_initial = 1700 MeV - 1600 MeV = 100 MeV.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: An alpha particle is fired directly head-on at a stationary, heavy gold nucleus (¹⁹⁷₇₉Au). The alpha particle comes to a momentary halt at a distance of closest approach d₀, and then repels backward. If the initial kinetic energy of the fired alpha particle is mathematically doubled, what will happen to the new distance of closest approach?
options: It will be reduced by a factor of 4.
It will be reduced by a factor of √2.
questions.explanation: At the exact distance of closest approach (d₀), all initial kinetic energy (K) is converted into electrostatic potential energy (U). K = U = (1 / 4πε₀) * ((2e)(Ze) / d₀). Rearranging gives d₀ = (1 / 4πε₀) * (2Ze² / K). This equation shows that d₀ is strictly inversely proportional to the initial kinetic energy K. If K is doubled, d₀ is perfectly halved.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Atomic masses and composition of nucleus
questions.question: The measured binding energy of a stable Deuteron (²₁H) is 2.23 MeV. Given the rest mass of a free proton is 1.0078 u and a free neutron is 1.0087 u, what is the exact calculated rest mass of the bound Deuteron nucleus? (1 u = 931.5 MeV)
questions.explanation: The binding energy (BE) is generated by the mass defect: BE = Δm × 931.5 MeV/u. Mass defect Δm = 2.23 MeV / 931.5 MeV/u ≈ 0.002394 u ≈ 0.0024 u. The mass defect represents the mass lost when assembling the nucleus: Δm = (m_p + m_n) - M_Deuteron. Substitute knowns: 0.0024 = (1.0078 + 1.0087) - M_Deuteron = 2.0165 - M_Deuteron. Therefore, M_Deuteron = 2.0165 - 0.0024 = 2.0141 u.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Radioactive Isotope P decays directly into Isotope Q with a decay constant λ. Isotope Q is highly unstable and rapidly decays into stable Isotope R with a decay constant 2λ. If a sealed sample starts purely as Isotope P at t=0, at what exact time t will the internal population of Isotope Q reach its absolute maximum value?
questions.explanation: This represents a standard series decay chain. The population of intermediate Isotope Q is governed by the Bateman equation: N_Q(t) =[λ_P N₀ / (λ_Q - λ_P)] * (e^(-λ_P t) - e^(-λ_Q t)). To find the maximum, set dN_Q/dt = 0, yielding λ_P e^(-λ_P t) = λ_Q e^(-λ_Q t). Taking natural log: ln(λ_P) - λ_P t = ln(λ_Q) - λ_Q t ⟹ t_max = ln(λ_Q / λ_P) / (λ_Q - λ_P). Substitute λ_P = λ and λ_Q = 2λ: t_max = ln(2λ / λ) / (2λ - λ) = (ln 2) / λ.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A stationary Uranium-232 (²³²₉₂U) nucleus spontaneously undergoes alpha decay to Thorium-228. The total energy released in this reaction (the Q-value) is precisely 5.40 MeV. In order to conserve linear momentum, the daughter nucleus must recoil. Taking this recoil into strict account, what is the exact kinetic energy imparted specifically to the emitted alpha particle?
questions.explanation: In spontaneous alpha decay from rest, total energy Q is partitioned into kinetic energy of the alpha particle (K_α) and recoiling daughter (K_daughter). To conserve momentum, K_α = (M_daughter / M_parent) * Q. Using mass numbers as highly accurate approximations for mass: Parent A_p = 232, Daughter A_d = 228. K_α = (228 / 232) × 5.40 MeV ≈ 0.98275 × 5.40 ≈ 5.307 MeV.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A specialized nuclear reactor continuously produces a specific radioactive isotope at a strictly constant rate of R₀ nuclei per second. The produced isotope is highly radioactive and decays with a constant λ. If the reactor starts at t=0 with absolutely none of this isotope present, what is the exact mathematical expression for the number of nuclei N(t) of this isotope present at any time t?
questions.explanation: This models radioactive growth. The net rate of change of N is the rate of production minus the rate of decay: dN/dt = R₀ - λN. Rearranging: dN / (R₀ - λN) = dt. Integrating both sides from t=0 (N=0) to t (N=N): -(1/λ) ln(R₀ - λN) |₀^N = t ⟹ ln((R₀ - λN) / R₀) = -λt. This simplifies to 1 - λN/R₀ = e^(-λt) ⟹ N(t) = (R₀ / λ)(1 - e^(-λt)).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: An isotropic point source of alpha particles has a steady radioactive activity of A₀ Becquerels (decays per second), emitting uniformly in all 3D spherical directions. A flat, circular radiation detector with a physical surface area S is placed directly facing the source at a distance d (where d ≫ √S). Assuming the detector operates with 100% detection efficiency and no alpha particles are absorbed by the air, what is the exact expected count rate registered by the detector?
questions.explanation: The isotropic point source uniformly emits A₀ alpha particles perfectly in all 3D directions every second. Imagine a massive hypothetical sphere of radius d completely surrounding the point source. The total surface area of this sphere is 4πd². All A₀ particles pass through this enormous area. The flat detector forms a tiny patch of area S on this sphere. The fraction of total particles striking it is the ratio of its area to the total spherical area: Fraction = S / 4πd². Therefore, the count rate registered is exactly A₀ × (S / 4πd²).
